Of course, that is not at all true and it
should be
obvious to anyone that this Company cannot give any assurances
as to what action the United States Government will take on any given
question.
If this were a signed contract this criticism might be serious,
but inasmuch as it is merely an unilateral permit and bears no evidence of
having been negotisted, I assume that we cannot be held responsible by
anyone for the language it contains.
I have just received your long and very interesting personal
letter of September 21 discussing a number of confidential subjects.
This
Letter was mailed, of course, before you learned that ir• Trippe was himself
going to the Far Last. It will be a great help to you, I am sure, to nave
the opportunity to cover these important matters with him personally and
I shall be much interested to learn of his reactions and what yau decide to
do. I have no comment to make and I am entirely in agreement with all of
your observations except that I am a little bit sceptical with regard to
your listing as one of our assets in CNAC "our interest in Route 5."
Due to our failure during the last three years to conclude any permanent
or long term agreement with CNAC covering the operations of Route 3 it woudd
seem that our interest in Route 3 is wholly dependent upon a temporary
operating agreement, cancellable by our Chinese friends on 30 days! notice.
This seems to be a rather precarious ground for bargain and sale.
I refer now to your letter of September 26, addressed to Mr. Van
Zandt with regard to the extension of Imperial and K.N.I.L.M. to Maniln, in
which you make the suggestion that it would be a good thing if we could
arrange to have the Philippine domestic lines, with our participation,
meet the foreign airlines outside the Philippines or possibly you also
have in mind meeting the foreign airlines at a port of entry on the south
coast of the Philippine Islands.
With regard to this plan, I would like to
submit a thought:
The establishment of a precedent in the Philippines
under which foreign international operators would be compelled to turn over
their traffic to Philippine domestic companies at a point just outside the
Philippines or on the coast (border) might be very embarrassing so far as
Pan American Airweys System as a whole is concerned.
You can readily see
that if this practice were adopted by just a few countries in our Latin
American field, it might paralize our whole system. It is, in fact, our
No. 1 nightmare that someday we may be faced with the demand that our
international planes stop at a frontier and turn over the traffic to a
domestic company to carry through that country and turn over in turn to a
domestic company of the next country and so on. I do not need to elaborate
on this as you can readily think it out for yourself.
